title: Inverter-based OTA
description: A complementary common-source (inverter) transconductor: an NMOS and a PMOS input device stacked between the rails share the same bias current, and their gates tie together as the input. Because both devices transconduct the input, the composite transconductance is the sum $g_{m,tot} = g_{m,n} + g_{m,p}$ — current reuse buys roughly double the $g_m$ for the same current, so the effective $g_m/I_D$ is $(g_m/I_D)_n + (g_m/I_D)_p$. Gain is $g_{m,tot}/(g_{ds,n} + g_{ds,p})$ and, for the same current, the input-referred thermal density is below a single device's, by $\sqrt{2}$ where the two transconductances are equal. The two gates are one node and the two sources are the two rails, so the gate-source voltages add up to the supply, $V_{GS,n} + |V_{GS,p}| = V_{DD}$: one inversion level is a choice and the other follows from it. The sheet is drawn that way. The NMOS is sized from the bias current and its $g_m/I_D$, and its gate-source voltage is the input level $V_{in}$; the PMOS carries the same current at the gate-source voltage the supply leaves above $V_{in}$, and its width is whatever that takes. On a process whose two thresholds add up to well under the supply the PMOS is left a large overdrive and sits deep in strong inversion, narrow and with little of the transconductance; on one whose thresholds nearly fill the supply both devices sit in moderate inversion. The cost is supply sensitivity: the bias current and hence $g_m$ depend directly on VDD, so the inverter needs a replica or common-mode bias loop and has poor native PSRR — sim owns the supply rejection. The PMOS device takes a sign param like the mirror-load convention so it can be sized on either an N-style or a signed-PMOS table. The shared input gate is a port: whatever drives the input has to hold it at the level the NMOS sets, and the output is held at $V_{out,dc}$ by the application's feedback. Held fixed and asked about at another process condition, the inverter keeps its supply: each device keeps its width, the PMOS keeps the gate voltage the supply leaves above the input, and a hold on $I_{bias}$, the balance of the two devices' currents, solves the bias current again so the two devices carry one current.

params.name: Av_target
params.note: DC gain target: 30 (about 30 dB) for a complementary single stage, whose two output conductances in parallel set it, the class of a low-power switched-capacitor integrator or a transconductor. An example, to be replaced with the design's own spec

params.name: GBW_target
params.note: unity-gain bandwidth target into the 2 pF load: current reuse roughly doubles the transconductance a given current buys, so an inverter-based OTA reaches about twice what a single-device stage does on the same supply current. An example, to be replaced with the design's own spec

params.name: SR_target
params.note: slew-rate target: 8 V/us moves a 0.5 V step in about 60 ns, in keeping with the bandwidth current reuse buys. An example, to be replaced with the design's own spec

params.name: vn_target
params.note: input-referred thermal density budget (the current-reuse benefit should beat a single device)

params.name: V_out_dc
params.note: output DC level (mid-supply for symmetric swing); sets both devices' vds. The two devices meet at a high-impedance output that nothing on this sheet holds; the feedback the application closes around the amplifier holds it (a common-mode feedback loop in a pseudo-differential build), and that loop is not on this sheet

params.name: sign_p
params.note: sign convention of the PMOS table's voltage axes: +1 for an N-style axis, -1 for a signed-PMOS axis. The PMOS's drain-source and gate-source voltages are both passed in it

params.name: I_bias
params.note: the single current shared by the N and P devices (current reuse), typed into the NMOS where the design is sized; the PMOS reads the NMOS's current there. Where the design is held fixed — another process condition — the supply is what stays put: the PMOS keeps the gate voltage the supply leaves above the input, and this current is solved again, between min and max, so that the two devices carry one current

params.name: gm_id_n
params.note: NMOS inversion — the one inversion level this sheet chooses. It sets the input level, and through it the PMOS: a higher gm/ID here lowers the input level and hands the PMOS more gate-source voltage, pushing it further into strong inversion

doc.title: NMOS input device
doc.description: The common-source NMOS half of the inverter; its source at ground, drain at the output DC level.

doc.title: PMOS input device
doc.description: The common-source PMOS half of the inverter; its source at VDD, drain at the output DC level. It carries the NMOS's current (current reuse) and its gate is the NMOS's gate, so its gate-source voltage is what the supply leaves above the input level and its width is what carries that current there. Its inversion level is read off the table, not chosen.

params.name: vgs_d
params.note: the supply down to the shared gate, signed to this table's axis convention

equations.name: V_in
equations.note: the input level this design sits at — the voltage on the gate the two devices share. The NMOS's source is at ground, so it is the NMOS's gate-source voltage, and the PMOS is sized at what the supply leaves above it. An OUTPUT of the NMOS's sizing, not a setting: whatever drives the input has to sit here

equations.name: gm_tot
equations.note: current reuse: both devices transconduct the input, so their gm add

equations.name: gm_id_eff
equations.note: effective composite gm/ID: the NMOS's chosen gm/ID plus the gm/ID the PMOS lands at — the current-reuse efficiency win

equations.name: Rout
equations.note: the resistance this stage presents at its output — both devices' output conductances in parallel. The gain assumes a capacitive load, so nothing here models a resistive one; this equation is what a composing parent checks its own loading against

equations.name: Av
equations.note: composite transconductance into the two output conductances in parallel

equations.name: vn_in
equations.note: each device's own drain-noise density summed in current and referred by gm_tot — both devices are counted. Below a single device at the same current, by sqrt(2) where the two transconductances are equal

equations.name: vos
equations.expr: sqrt((pelgrom_vos(avt, abeta, n__W, L_n, n__gm_id)*n__gm)^2 + (pelgrom_vos(avt, abeta, p__W, L_p, p__gm_id)*p__gm)^2)/gm_tot
equations.note: estimate: the N and P mismatch offsets, input-referred, each weighted by its device's share of the composite transconductance, as the noise equation weights each device's noise. An offset at one device's gate moves the output current by that device's gm, and the input sees gm_tot, so a device with little of the transconductance contributes little of the offset. Adding the two unweighted would overstate it

equations.name: cgg_in
equations.note: estimate: the capacitance the input terminal presents. Both gates are driven together, so both gate capacitances load the driver. Gate capacitance only, because the Miller term needs the gate-drain fraction and these tables do not carry it — and here the drain swings against the gate, so that omission is at its worst. No check reads it

equations.name: I_q
equations.note: estimate: quiescent supply current — a single inverter leg as these equations model it; a pseudo-differential realization doubles it. The datasheet line for comparing designs; no check reads it

checks.note: reads each device's thermal noise from the table where the table carries it, and the gamma = 1 estimate where it does not; it stays advisory because a sheet cannot know which table it will be evaluated on, and the simulator owns noise sign-off
the stacked N and P must both stay saturated between the rails with a little margin
estimate: very high composite gm/ID means weak inversion and strong VDD dependence of the bias — budget a common-mode bias loop; sim owns PSRR
